name: Modern Bloom Filters (save-buffer benchmark suite)
workload: insert/query cycles-per-op on random 64-bit hashes at 1% target FPR, progressing from a naive Bloom filter through blocked, register-blocked/SIMD (AVX2), and bit-pattern (with mask rotation) variants
claimed_speedup: naive Bloom filter: ~56-254 cycles/op -> blocked: ~30 cycles/op -> register-blocked AVX2: ~5 cycles/op (4x faster than the non-SIMD register-blocked version) -> bit-pattern SIMD ('ultimate' filter): ~2.5 cycles/op, a 22x overall throughput increase over the classic Bloom filter
tradeoffs: the fastest variant trades a higher, less predictable false-positive rate and requires AVX2; bit-pattern approach needs a precomputed mask table
caveats: Underlying repo (save-buffer/bloomfilter_benchmarks) is on the excluded KNOWN_LIST, but this blog post is a first-party Tier-A benchmark write-up (public code, compiler+flags+CPU stated) for that known project, so reported per the exception rule with is_evidence_for_known=true; blog's own GitHub Pages URL (save-buffer.github.io/bloom_filter.html) permanently redirects to blog.krassovsky.com, the author's personal domain -- both opened and confirmed identical content
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia query "bloom filter faster" surfaced 'Modern Bloom Filters: 22x Faster' (2023-05-30) -> opened blog post directly

name: Bumped Ribbon Retrieval (BuRR) / homogeneous ribbon filter
workload: Static AMQ / retrieval data structure benchmark on synthetic key sets, measuring space overhead and construction/query throughput against Bloom, Cuckoo, and Xor filters
claimed_speedup: BuRR achieves space overhead well below 1% vs Bloom filter's >=44% overhead and is described as faster than classical Bloom filters; the faster ribbon variants are only moderately slower than Bloom/Xor in query while having at least an order of magnitude smaller space overhead
hardware: AMD EPYC 7702, 64 cores, 2.0GHz base / 3.35GHz boost, 1TiB DDR4-3200, Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: Static/immutable; construction is a banded linear-algebra solve rather than simple hashing, which is more complex to implement/port than Bloom hashing
caveats: lorenzhs/burr is already on the known-catalogued list; included here only as additional Tier A evidence per the assignment's exception rule, since the paper provides a fully reproducible benchmark (public code, stated compiler/flags/hardware) directly targeting the Bloom/Cuckoo/Xor baselines.
found_via: arXiv API search all:ribbon OR filter OR approximate OR membership -> arXiv:2109.01892 'Fast Succinct Retrieval and Approximate Membership using Ribbon'

name: PGM-index
workload: Point lookups (10M queries) over 200M 64-bit keys from the amzn SOSD dataset, comparing tuned PGM-index against a tuned STX B-Tree and other index structures.
claimed_speedup: 326.48 ns/lookup (14.0 MB) for PGM vs 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB) for BTree on the amzn dataset -> ~1.5x lower latency at ~12x less space (derived from page data, Table 2)
tradeoffs: Supports updates (unlike RS), multi-level piecewise-linear error-bounded structure; PGM has the fewest cache misses per second under multithreading in the SOSD study but showed only a 27x speedup at 40 threads vs FAST's 32x.
caveats: PGM-index's canonical repo (https://github.com/gvinciguerra/PGM-index) is already in the excluded/known list for this run. This entry only reports NEW Tier B evidence found this session (the SOSD VLDB'21 paper's direct latency/size comparison against STX B-Tree), so it is flagged is_evidence_for_known=true rather than skipped, per the harness exception rule.
found_via: SOSD VLDB'21 paper (http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p1-marcus.pdf, Table 2) opened while researching RMI/RadixSpline; PGM-index metadata via gh api repos/gvinciguerra/PGM-index

name: Badger
workload: WiscKey-style key/value-separated LSM benchmark on an AWS i3.large instance (2 vCPU, 15.25GB RAM, 450GB local NVMe SSD, ~100K random-read IOPS at 4KB via fio): loaded 250M x 128B values (35GB), 75M x 1KB values (73GB), and 5M x 16KB values (76GB), each keyed by 22-byte keys, sized so the dataset does not fit entirely in RAM in either engine; measured data-loading time/output size, random Get, and sorted-range Iterate.
claimed_speedup: Random key lookup (Get) at least 3.5x faster than RocksDB (Badger's LSM tree is small enough to fit in RAM); data loading 4.5x faster at 1KB values and 11.7x faster at 16KB values (0.86x-14x faster overall depending on value size, with small values ~2-3x slower); ~4x faster Get overall and an estimated 86% lower AWS instance cost due to running on cheap NVMe storage instead of large-RAM RocksDB instances. Iterate (range scan) is slower than RocksDB.
hardware: AWS i3.large: 2 vCPU, 15.25GB RAM, 450GB local NVMe SSD
stars_or_usage: 15,773 stars; storage engine of the Dgraph graph database
tradeoffs: Pure Go (no cgo dependency on RocksDB's C++), based on the WiscKey key/value-separation design; slower than RocksDB for sorted range iteration; value-log design means space amplification/GC tuning matters for update-heavy workloads.
caveats: This is dgraph's own first-party benchmark; instance type (AWS i3.large) is stated but the exact CPU model and Go compiler version are not, so it falls short of Tier A. The original open.dgraph.io post is dead; content recovered via Wayback Machine (2017 snapshot). Benchmark harness (dgraph-io/badger-bench) and raw logs are linked from the post as public artifacts. Numbers are from 2017, an early Badger version; current Badger performance characteristics may differ.
found_via: Blogs / talks: HN Algolia search "Badger key value store dgraph" -> dgraph engineering blog post "Badger – A fast key-value store written natively in Go" (open.dgraph.io/post/badger/, 2017), recovered via web.archive.org since the original domain no longer serves the post.

name: TidesDB (seek/range-query benchmark vs RocksDB)
workload: 5 million point-seek operations, 8 concurrent threads, 16-byte keys / 100-byte values, sync disabled, TidesDB v6.1.0 vs RocksDB v10.7.5.
claimed_speedup: 4.17x faster random seeks (3.73M vs 893K ops/sec, 2us vs 8us median latency), 4.74x faster sequential seeks, 5.25x faster Zipfian-distributed seeks; range-query performance described as "competitive but not dominant" versus RocksDB
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700K (8 cores/16 threads) @4.9GHz, 48GB DDR4, Western Digital Blue 3D NAND 500GB SATA SSD, Ubuntu 23.04 x86_64, kernel 6.2.0-39-generic
tradeoffs: Aggressively keeps SSTable metadata (block indices, bloom filters, min/max keys, file handles) resident in memory to eliminate disk I/O on the seek path, trading memory footprint for latency; CPU utilization is higher than RocksDB in the same test (469% vs 635%—note TidesDB is actually lower here).
caveats: TidesDB itself is already catalogued (KNOWN_LIST); this entry records a new, higher-quality Tier A benchmark for it discovered via its own blog (surfaced through Hacker News), separate from its repo README. Raw benchmark report and benchtool source are linked from the article. The author's own "Honest Assessment" section notes range queries are not a clear win.
found_via: HN Algolia: query="faster than RocksDB" tags=story -> https://tidesdb.com/articles/benchmark-design-range-seek-tidesdb610-rocksdb1075

name: Zenoh (throughput/latency study vs MQTT, Kafka, DDS)
workload: Pub/sub throughput (msg/s and bit/s) and ping-pong latency across payload sizes 8B-512MiB on single-machine and multi-machine (100GbE) setups, comparing Zenoh 0.7.0-rc, Mosquitto MQTT 2.0.15, Kafka broker 3.2.1 (rdkafka client), and Eclipse Cyclone DDS.
claimed_speedup: Zenoh peer-mode ~60-65x Kafka msg/s and ~55-65x Kafka bit/s at 8B payload (single- and multi-machine); ~12x Kafka at 32KiB payload; Kafka saturates at ~53-62K msg/s / 3-5 Gbps vs Zenoh's >4M msg/s / up to 67 Gbps
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X @ fixed 4.0 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS; multi-machine scenario used 100 Gb Ethernet
tradeoffs: Zenoh is a decentralized pub/sub protocol (no broker required in peer mode), different architecture/consistency model than Kafka's replicated commit log; Kafka bindings used (rdkafka) failed above 1MB messages, capping Kafka's tested range and possibly disadvantaging it at large payloads
caveats: Authors are Zenoh/Zettascale-affiliated (first-party for the winning system), so treat as a vendor-run comparison though methodology, code, and hardware are public; Kafka tuned per online docs rather than by Kafka experts; arXiv preprint, not confirmed peer-reviewed; is_evidence_for_known applies since eclipse-zenoh/zenoh is already catalogued
